EVIDENCE / SCIENTIFIC METHOD

Digital Evidence and Computer Crime

Eoghan Casey
SYLLABUS READING GUIDE

Digital Evidence and Computer Crime

Eoghan Casey

3rd edition · 2011 · Academic Press / Elsevier

A foundational text on forensic science, digital investigation, offender analysis, and network evidence. Especially valuable for learning to reason from artifacts rather than merely operate software.

Publisher’s editionPrint guide
The route below follows the third edition’s verified early chapters and major subject areas; it is not a complete publisher TOC. The US and European legal chapters require current Indian-law supplementation.
READ WITH A QUESTION IN MIND

Your chapter connections.

12 study sections
01

1. Foundations of Digital Forensics

Define digital evidence, core principles, the cybertrail, and the challenges of applying forensic science to changing technology.

2.4 · Nature and Characteristics of Digital Evidence3.7 · Introduction to Digital Forensics
02

2. Language of Computer Crime Investigation

Build a precise vocabulary for systems, roles, and the relationship between computers and crime.

1.1 · Introduction to Law and Cyberspace1.5 · Types of Internet Crimes and Cyber Offences
03

3. Digital Evidence in the Courtroom

Study expert duties, admissibility, certainty, circumstantial evidence, and presentation.

2.9 · Admissibility of Electronic Evidence4.10 · Digital Evidence Presentation Techniques4.12 · Courtroom Presentation and Expert Testimony
04

4–5. Cybercrime Law

Compare the book’s US and European legal discussions, then identify the corresponding Indian questions without assuming equivalence.

1.3 · Cyber Jurisprudence: Meaning and Scope1.12 · International Cyber Regulations: NIST and ENISA Standards
05

6. Conducting Digital Investigations

Use process models, investigative scaffolding, and the scientific method to organize a case.

2.2 · Stages of Cyber Crime Investigation Process3.7 · Introduction to Digital Forensics
06

7. Handling a Digital Crime Scene

Study authorization, preparation, survey, and preservation. Apply the concepts through the acquisition simulation.

2.3 · Legal Framework for Cyber Crime Investigation2.6 · Collection and Preservation of Digital Evidence
07

8. Investigative Reconstruction with Digital Evidence

Evaluate equivocal artifacts, victimology, scene characteristics, and threshold assessments.

4.7 · Memory and Log Analysis4.11 · Appreciation and Evaluation of Digital Evidence
08

9. Modus Operandi, Motive, and Technology

Connect modus operandi and motive to technical choices while keeping inference separate from observation.

3.7 · Introduction to Digital Forensics5.3 · Threat Hunting and Threat Analysis
09

10. Violent Crime and Digital Evidence

Examine the role of digital traces in serious-crime reconstruction and the need for careful interpretation.

2.5 · Sources of Electronic Evidence4.11 · Appreciation and Evaluation of Digital Evidence
10

11. Digital Evidence as Alibi

Test time-based claims and alternative explanations rather than assuming every account event identifies a person.

2.4 · Nature and Characteristics of Digital Evidence4.7 · Memory and Log Analysis
11

Computer-system examination

Read the operating-system and device chapters relevant to your evidence source. Preserve format, timestamp, and application context.

3.8 · Device and Computer Forensics3.10 · Mobile Forensics4.5 · Disk Analysis using DEFT
12

Network and internet evidence

Connect the book’s network-layer discussions to current packet, flow, cloud, and provider evidence. Update older tool assumptions.

3.9 · Network Forensics3.12 · Cloud Forensics4.8 · Network Traffic Analysis using DEFT Tools
